rubric: Review the essential mathematical argument, allowing equivalent local equality-transport encodings such as rewrite versus f_equal/exact or symmetry. FAITHFUL requires a verified proof preserving the main strategy, supplied-premise use, and any specified induction variable/cases. PARTIAL represents meaningful reference steps but has missing or incorrect steps. DIVERGENT follows a different main strategy or invents premises, whether or not the theorem is verified. UNASSESSABLE has no interpretable formal argument. This semantic review is broader than the deterministic exact-structure proxy and is an assistant judgment, not independent human review. Theorem-only outputs are compared to the same hidden reference; a match does not demonstrate use of its English input.

reviews.rationale: Invents a premise H and attempts rewriting. The theorem has no premise, and the supplied argument uses definitional reduction.
Attempts to introduce and rewrite a nonexistent premise instead of reducing the two successor clauses.
Rewrites an undeclared H. It does not implement the supplied definitional computation of 3 + n.
Attempts induction with a failed rewrite rather than the reference definitional reduction. No induction is required or supplied in the reference.
Invents an equality premise H instead of reducing the two left-zero additions.
Invents H and rewrites it; this does not implement the reference definitional argument.
Uses the supplied equality and symmetry, but leaves the reflexive goal open. It does not complete the reference premise-reuse argument.

Verified reverse equality from the same supplied premise. Rewriting S n to m and closing m = m is an equivalent local equality-transport encoding of the reference symmetry argument; the exact tactic sequence differs.

Verified transport of n = m through both successor contexts. A direct rewrite replaces the two explicit f_equal steps; it preserves the same local congruence argument at the semantic granularity of this review.
Verified use of the premise under two successors. Direct rewriting is an equivalent local congruence encoding, although the stricter structural proxy differs.
Introduces the variables and premise, rewrites the assumed sum from left to right beneath successor, and closes by reflexivity, matching the supplied argument.
Uses exactly the reference left-to-right premise rewrite and reflexive closing step; the reference informal argument was hidden in this condition.
Introduces the right premise but rewrites it in the wrong direction. The supplied argument explicitly requires replacing n by zero, and the generated proof fails.
Attempts premise-based rewriting but uses 0 -> n instead of n -> 0, so it cannot perform the reference reduction and fails verification.

Verified induction on n with the same base case and induction hypothesis. Rewriting IH inside the successor instead of f_equal followed by exact IH is an equivalent implementation of the same successor-step congruence.
Verified induction on the same variable with the reference base and successor cases. The local IH use is encoded as rewriting rather than f_equal/exact.
Matches the reference induction on n, zero simplification, and successor rewrite with IH. Rocq verifies the proof.
Attempts simplification and reflexivity with no induction. This omits the essential reference induction and fails on symbolic right-zero additions.
Attempts induction on n, but omits introductions for m and the premise and uses reflexivity instead of the supplied premise in the base case. The intended argument is only partially represented.
A valid direct-rewrite proof, but it omits the induction explicitly required by the reference argument. Correctness does not imply fidelity here.

Copies an induction skeleton but intros b actually names the first quantified variable a; the other binders and premise are omitted. It does not implement induction on the intended second binder or premise-based base case.
Attempts a direct premise rewrite that does not match a subterm, omitting the required induction on b and failing verification.
Attempts the intended induction on n with an IH rewrite, but leaves m and p unintroduced. The script violates the fixed induction contract and does not complete a valid formalization.
Invents an extra premise H and tries rewriting instead of the supplied induction/reassociation argument.
